title: Maksoin yli tuhat euroa turhaan
subtitle: I paid over a thousand euros for nothing

blocks.text: This corpus is full of precise numbers — 161,16 euroa, kolme kertaa, viisi vuotta — because Finnish reviewers treat exact figures as evidence. You've been skipping past every number so far. Today you stop skipping.

blocks.translation: I paid over a thousand euros for nothing.

blocks.title: Numbers as proof
blocks.text: When a reviewer states a specific figure — 161,16 euroa, not just 'a lot' — it functions as documentation, almost like showing a receipt inside the sentence. Precise numbers are one of the ways these reviews establish credibility, especially in complaints that end up disputed.
Piece 2 — Money: numbers force the partitive

blocks.content: From Lesson 10 you know the partitive marks 'some of' a group. Numbers two and above trigger this same partitive on the noun that follows them: viisi {euroa|grammar|partitive singular|euros} (five euros), sata {euroa|grammar|partitive singular|euros} (a hundred euros). Only yksi (one) keeps the noun in its plain form: yksi euro.

blocks.text: Piece 3 — Kertaa: counting how many times

blocks.title: Kerta and its partitive kertaa
blocks.text: Kerta means 'a time/occasion'. Following the same rule as Piece 2, after a number it takes the partitive form {kertaa|grammar|partitive singular|times}: kolme kertaa, 'three times'. This is exactly how the corpus describes a car towed repeatedly: autoni hinattiin kolme kertaa (Lesson 14) — now you know why kertaa ends the way it does.

items.en: My car was towed three times.

lines.fi: Maksoin yli tuhat euroa turhaan. Auto hinattiin kolme kertaa.
lines.en: I paid over a thousand euros for nothing. The car was towed three times.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fi: Kuinka monta vuotta olet käynyt siellä?
lines.en: How many years have you been going there?

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: One rule covers almost every number phrase you'll meet: number two or higher + noun in the partitive. Viisi euroa, kolme kertaa, viisi vuotta — same shape every time. Only yksi breaks the pattern by keeping the plain form. Learn that single exception and the rest is automatic.

blocks.content: Tuhat: TU-hat (two syllables, soft 'h'). Kertaa: KER-taa (long final 'aa', held clearly — this length is what marks it as partitive rather than plain kerta). Euroa: EU-ro-a (the 'eu' glides like 'eh-oo' run together, not English 'you').

rows.en: euros (partitive singular of euro, after numbers 2+)

blocks.title: What you now own
items: cardinal numbers 1-10, plus sata (hundred) and tuhat (thousand)
the rule: numbers 2+ force the partitive singular on the following noun
kertaa — times, and vuotta — years, both explained via that same rule
